method: A daylight-saving transition is the instant a zone swaps between its standard and summer offsets. The offset of a zone at an instant is read from the browser's Intl.DateTimeFormat: the zone's wall clock is formatted at that instant, that wall clock is reinterpreted as UTC, and the difference gives the offset. A change is located by sampling the offset every six hours across the requested year plus three days of margin on each side, then bisecting between the last instant on the old offset and the first on the new one down to the millisecond; only changes whose local date falls inside the year are kept. The skipped or repeated hour is the wall clock at the change instant measured with the old offset, and the other side is the wall clock at the same instant under the new offset, so a spring change reads 02:00 to 03:00 and an autumn change 02:00 to 01:00. A zone that shifts at local midnight names the earlier date on the new side. Offsets, dates and shift sizes are exactly what the IANA database copy inside the browser reports: historical years come from its back-zone data and future years from its projection of legislation as of that copy, so a later statutory change cannot appear here until the browser's copy is updated. Everything runs locally; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent.

sources.title: IANA Time Zone Database — the tz database of zone offsets and daylight-saving transitions that the browser's Intl support uses
